title: LinkedIn games analysis pipeline
text:
This is a personal project to create a live analysis pipeline that will show descriptive analysis of daily LinkedIn games records between PM and CW.
This pipeline will serve to elucidate who is the better overall player in LinkedIn games (Tango, Zip, Pinpoint and Cross climb) to date; between players PM and CW. Beginning from April 29th till today, August 06, 2026, data will continually be updated manually in the raw .xlsx file and ran through the pipeline for analysis when rendered.
In addition to summarizing means, medians, standard deviations, and visualizing score distributions over time, this document also employs Bayesian independent‐samples t‐tests for each game type to quantify the strength of evidence for performance differences between PM and CW. In each case, Bayes factors (BF10) is computed along with prior and posterior distributions plotted to illustrate how observed data update our beliefs about any effect (see Note 1 below).
This document aims to describe, visualize, and evaluate, using both descriptive statistics and Bayesian hypothesis tests, to assess the differences in scores between the two players.
# Libraries utilized
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(car)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(BayesFactor)

# Load the data in
dat <- read_xlsx("LinkedIn_games_data.xlsx")
To account for missing data (e.g., failure to complete Pinpoint guesses), “-” will be recoded into N.A. and listwise deletion will be conducted to remove the data for the day. Additionally, since the data is manually entered, it is recorded in wide format. The code below pivots the wide format into long format, which is simpler for analysis.
Show the code
# Convert "-" into NA and all columns into double
dat <- dat %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(., "-"))) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.double)) 

# Change to long format
dat_long <- dat %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = c("Player", "Game_type"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "value"
  )

Homogenity of Variance Assumptions
Runs Levene’s test as a check of homogenity of variance for each game type subsets. Although Bayesian t‐tests are typically robust to mild heterogeneity of variance, it remains good practice to understand whether this assumption might be violated.

TangoZipPinpointCrossclimb




Show the code
# Levene's test of homogenity of variance
levene_T <- leveneTest(value ~ as.factor(Player), data = dat_longT)
levene_T_df <- as.data.frame(levene_T)

# Clean up df formatting
levene_T_df <- levene_T_df %>% 
  mutate(
    `Df` = Df,
    `F Value` = round(`F value`, 3),
    `Pr(>F)` = signif(`Pr(>F)`, 3)
  ) %>% 
  select(`Df`, `F Value`, `Pr(>F)`)

# Create Clean table
levene_T_df %>% 
  kable(
    caption = "Levene’s Test for Homogeneity of Variance",
    col.names = c("Degrees of Freedom", "F Statistic", "p-value"),
    format = "html"
  ) %>% 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center", bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

text:
Bayes Factor computation

TangoZipPinpointCrossclimb


Bayes factor computation for Tango between PM and CW.


Show the code
# Filter out PM’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_pm <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "PM", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Filter out CW’s values (remove NA from 'value')
tango_cw <- dat_longT %>%
  filter(Player == "CW", !is.na(value)) %>%
  pull(value)

# Run Bayesian two-sample t-test
bf_obj_tango <- ttestBF(
  x = tango_pm,
  y = tango_cw,
  paired = FALSE
)

# extractBF() returns a data frame; the “bf” column is the numeric Bayes Factor
bf_tango <- extractBF(bf_obj_tango)$bf[1]

# Build a simple one‐row data.frame for kable()
data.frame(
  "Game Type" = "Tango",
  "BF10"      = round(bf_tango, 3),
  "Notes"     = if (bf_tango > 1) {
                   "Evidence favoring difference (H1)"
                 } else {
                   "Evidence favoring H0 or inconclusive"
                 }
) %>%
  # Display as HTML table with caption and styling
  kable(
    caption   = "Bayesian independent‐samples t‐test (Tango)",
    col.names = c("Game Type", "BF₁₀", "Notes"),
    format    = "html"
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    full_width        = FALSE,
    position          = "center",
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")
  )



Bayesian independent‐samples t‐test (Tango)


Game Type
BF₁₀
Notes




Tango
0.479

Visualizations of posterior and prior distributions.


Show the code
# Obtain 10,000 posterior samples of the standardized effect size (delta)
posterior_samples_T <- posterior(bf_obj_tango, iterations = 10000)

# Convert to a data frame for easier handling
posterior_df_T <- as.data.frame(posterior_samples_T)

# Create a sequence of effect size (delta) values for the prior
delta_range_T <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 1000)  # reasonable range for visualization

# Compute the density of the default Cauchy prior (scale = 0.707)
prior_density_T <- dcauchy(delta_range_T, location = 0, scale = sqrt(2) / 2)

# Create a data frame for the prior distribution
prior_df_T <- data.frame(
  delta = delta_range_T,
  density = prior_density_T,
  Distribution = "Prior"
)

# Compute the density of the posterior samples
posterior_density_T <- density(posterior_df_T$delta, adjust = 1.5)  # adjust can be tuned for smoothing

posterior_df_density_T <- data.frame(
  delta = posterior_density_T$x,
  density = posterior_density_T$y,
  Distribution = "Posterior"
)

# Combine prior and posterior data frames
combined_df_T <- rbind(prior_df_T, posterior_df_density_T)

# Plot both distributions
ggplot(combined_df_T, aes(x = delta, y = density, color = Distribution, fill = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.2, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Prior and Posterior Distributions of Effect Size (δ)",
    subtitle = "Tango: PM vs. CW",
    x = "Effect Size (δ)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Prior" = "#00CFC1", "Posterior" = "#FF6B5C")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
This document demonstrates a complete Bayesian analysis pipeline in R for a simple reaction time experiment with a 2×2 factorial design. The goal is to show, in a clear and reproducible way, how to move from a simulated dataset to a fitted Bayesian mixed-effects model, and then on to interpretation of the posterior, predictions, and basic hypothesis tests.
The focus here is practical. I assume you are comfortable with basic R, regression-type models, and the idea of random effects, but perhaps newer to Bayesian modelling with brms. Throughout, I explain the key Bayesian concepts that are directly relevant to the workflow, including priors, posterior distributions, mixed-effects modelling, and MCMC sampling.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Experimental Scenario
The example is grounded in a cognitive psychology setting. Imagine an experiment where participants respond to visual targets while two experimental factors are manipulated. The first factor is Viewing Condition, where participants either have a Restricted view or an Unrestricted view of some relevant aspect of the display. The second factor is Target Location, which can be Same or Different relative to a previous location.
The outcome of interest is reaction time (RT) in milliseconds. In line with typical inhibition-of-return paradigms, the data are simulated so that responses are slower when the target appears in the same location compared to a different one. The expected inhibition effect is around 20–30 ms. Viewing condition is not expected to have a strong effect, and there is no strong interaction between viewing condition and target location.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Setup and Data Generation
To begin, I load the necessary packages and set a seed for reproducibility. The main packages used are tidyverse for data handling, brms for the Bayesian modelling, bayestestR and bayesplot for working with the posterior, and tidybayes for tidy posterior extraction.

library(tidyverse) # Data wrangling and visualisation
library(brms) # Bayesian regression models (Stan backend)
library(bayestestR) # Posterior summaries and hypothesis tests
library(bayesplot) # Posterior visualisation tools
library(tidybayes) # Tidy extraction of posterior samples

set.seed(42)

Next, I create a trial-level dataset that reflects the 2×2 design and the expected pattern of means. 30 participants complete 24 trials per condition, producing a reasonably sized data set to resemble a modest laboratory sample.

# Parameters for simulation
n_subj   <- 30          # Number of participants
n_trials <- 24          # Trials per condition per participant

# Define cell means (ms), one row per condition so there's no risk of the
# means lining up with the wrong condition (expand.grid()'s row order isn't
# always what you'd guess - listing conditions explicitly avoids that trap)
# These values encode a ~25 ms inhibition effect for "Same" vs. "Different"
mu_table <- tribble(
  ~Viewing,       ~Location,    ~mean, ~sd,
  "Restricted",   "Same",         530,  30,
  "Restricted",   "Different",    505,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Same",         525,  30,
  "Unrestricted", "Different",    500,  30
)

# Generate trial-level data
dat <- expand.grid(
  Subj     = 1:n_subj,
  Viewing  = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted"),
  Location = c("Same", "Different"),
  Trial    = 1:n_trials
) %>%
  left_join(mu_table, by = c("Viewing", "Location")) %>%
  mutate(
    RT      = rnorm(n(), mean = mean, sd = sd),
    Subj    = factor(Subj),
    Viewing = factor(Viewing, levels = c("Restricted", "Unrestricted")),
    Location = factor(Location, levels = c("Different", "Same"))
  ) %>%
  select(Subj, Viewing, Location, Trial, RT)

head(dat, 12)

   Subj    Viewing Location Trial       RT
1     1 Restricted     Same     1 571.1288
2     2 Restricted     Same     1 513.0591
3     3 Restricted     Same     1 540.8939
4     4 Restricted     Same     1 548.9859
5     5 Restricted     Same     1 542.1280
6     6 Restricted     Same     1 526.8163
7     7 Restricted     Same     1 575.3457
8     8 Restricted     Same     1 527.1602
9     9 Restricted     Same     1 590.5527
10   10 Restricted     Same     1 528.1186
11   11 Restricted     Same     1 569.1461
12   12 Restricted     Same     1 598.5994


At this point, I briefly check that the simulation behaves as intended. The condition means should show longer RTs in the Same condition than in the Different condition, with only small differences between viewing conditions.

dat %>%
  group_by(Viewing, Location) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_RT = mean(RT),
    sd_RT   = sd(RT),
    n       = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Viewing      Location  mean_RT sd_RT     n
  <fct>        <fct>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 Restricted   Different    504.  28.3   720
2 Restricted   Same         530.  31.0   720
3 Unrestricted Different    499.  30.3   720
4 Unrestricted Same         526.  30.6   720


This simple summary reassures us that the simulated dataset captures the qualitative pattern we designed.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Priors
Before fitting, it’s worth being explicit about the priors. brms will pick default (flat or very weakly informative) priors automatically, but a Bayesian workflow is more transparent when priors are chosen deliberately. Here I use weakly informative priors centred on plausible values given the scale of the data (reaction times in the 400-600ms range, with an expected effect of a few tens of milliseconds):

Intercept: normal(500, 100) - centred on a plausible average RT, wide enough to not rule out much.
Fixed-effect coefficients (b): normal(0, 50) - centred on “no effect”, allowing effects up to roughly +/-100ms to be plausible a priori.
Residual and random-intercept SDs: exponential(1) - a standard weakly informative choice for scale parameters, keeping them positive and not too large.


priors <- c(
  prior(normal(500, 100), class = Intercept),
  prior(normal(0, 50),   class = b),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sigma),
  prior(exponential(1),  class = sd)
)

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Model fit

fit <- brm(
  formula = RT ~ Viewing * Location + (1 | Subj),
  data    = dat,
  family  = gaussian(),
  prior   = priors,
  chains  = 4,
  cores   = 4,
  iter    = 2000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  seed    = 42,
  backend = "rstan"
)

chains = 4 runs four independent MCMC chains so we can check they agree with each other (a key diagnostic for whether sampling has worked properly). warmup = 1000 discards the first 1000 iterations per chain while the sampler tunes itself, keeping the remaining 1000 per chain (4000 total) as usable posterior draws.

title: Bayesian Analysis of a 2×2 Factorial Reaction Time Experiment in R
text:
Visualizing the posterior
The plot below shows the posterior distribution for each fixed-effect coefficient - essentially, how much belief the model places on each possible effect size after seeing the data.

mcmc_plot(fit, type = "areas", variable = "^b_", regex = TRUE)




Posterior distributions of the fixed-effect coefficients.




tidybayes lets us extract the posterior draws for the effect we care most about - the difference in RT between the Same and Different location conditions (our simulated inhibition-of-return effect) - and plot its full distribution directly.

fit %>%
  spread_draws(b_LocationSame) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = b_LocationSame)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill = "#005F73") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Estimated effect of Same vs. Different location (ms)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Posterior distribution of the location effect"
  )




Posterior distribution of the Same vs. Different location effect (ms).

title: Ho Chin Wei
text:
I’m a PhD researcher in Psychology at the University of Hull, funded by the White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership (WRDTP). My work sits at the intersection of human cognition and artificial intelligence — I’m interested in how our minds adapt, resist, and evolve as AI becomes harder to tell apart from reality.
My MSc research (Distinction) explored how people judge the authenticity of AI-altered images: how we cognitively process AI-generated images differently from real photographs, and what happens when the line between the two blurs. My PhD is now extending that into joint-action settings, examining whether the social Inhibition of Return effect persists when the other actor in a task is an AI rather than a person. I’m also broadly interested in the wider social and philosophical fallout of an AI-saturated world — from AI-generated misinformation to what “real” and “fake” even mean anymore. (More of this shows up on my blog!)
Before Hull, I completed my BSc in Psychology at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, where I was twice named an NTU President Research Scholar through the Undergraduate Research Experience on Campus (URECA) programme, leading two independent, year-long research projects along the way. Full academic history is on my CV.
